newsitem.title: USA: Dow hits record, bonds fall before economic data.
newsitem.headline: Dow hits record, bonds fall before economic data.

text.p: The Dow Jones industrial average closed at a record for a second day in a row Tuesday, but bonds fell as the market braced for economic data due later this week.
The dollar edged higher as positive comments on European monetary union depressed the German mark, while a fire at a Japanese nuclear fuel processing plant weighed on the yen.

The Dow closed up 5.77 points at 7,085.16, beating Monday's record finish of 7,079.39. In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,290 to 1,180 on active volume of 491 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

"The market is very divided on the outlook for interest rate policy," said Charles White, managing director at Avatar Associates. "Right now there's no compelling evidence to drive us in either direction."
Investors were worried about Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's warnings recently that stocks could be overvalued and that the central bank might raise short-term interest rates.

In the bond market, the 30-year Treasury bond was off 14/32, or $4.375 per $1,000 face value, which raised its yield to 6.85 percent from Monday's close of 6.82 percent. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
Analysts said the market was likely to become even more cautious ahead of the meeting of the Fed's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) on March 25.
The latest economic data unnerved some investors.

The Labour Department said labour costs rose 2.5 percent in the fourth quarter after a 1.4 percent increase in the third quarter and productivity rose 1.1 percent after a 2.2 percent rise in the third quarter.
The numbers are closely watched since gains in productivity, which allow businesses to increase their output without raising their costs, are seen as crucial to containing inflation.
"Basically, this market has been put on wait," said Alfred Goldman, technical analyst at A.G. Edwards & Sons. "We're going to have more of this ragged action until we get past the FOMC meeting."
The dollar climbed as high as 1.7079 marks and 122.06 yen in Europe before retreating.
In late trading, the dollar fetched 1.7037 marks, up from 1.7015 marks late on Monday. The dollar rose to 121.78 Japanese yen from 121.63 yen.
Coffee and cocoa prices soared on fresh concern about short supplies.

At New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, cocoa prices jumped for the second day in a row and rose to the highest level in nearly seven months. May cocoa closed up $59 per metric ton at $1,451, up more than 4 percent on the day.
The day's high at $1,451 was the highest price for the May contract since Aug. 22, 1996.
Coffee prices also ended broadly higher on supply concerns with May coffee up 3.85 cents a pound at 203.15 cents.

Overseas, the FTSE soared at the opening but then gave back much of the gains, and ended up 6.9 points at 4,444.3, its sixth straight record. In Tokyo, the Nikkei 225 average rose 153.83 points to 18,267.72.
